name: Kadambavaneswarar Temple, Kulithalai
deity: Shiva as Kadambavaneswarar (Kadambanathar), with the goddess Mutrila Mulaiammai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine on the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); present structure largely Nayak-era over an earlier foundation
dynasty: Early Tamil Shaiva patrons; later Nayak-era rebuilding
summary: Kadambavaneswarar, Lord of the Kadamba Forest, graces the bank of the Kaveri at Kulithalai, the Tirukkadambanthurai of Appar's hymns, where a north-facing self-manifested Shiva is worshipped by seven celestial maidens standing behind him.

sections.history: Kulithalai, in Karur district, stands where the Kaveri runs broad and slow, and its old names speak of the river: Kadambanthurai, the landing of the kadamba grove, and Kuzhithandalai. In the Tevaram the shrine is Tirukkadambanthurai, praised in the hymns of Appar, and a temple listing adds the later poet Arunagirinathar among its devotees. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri in Chola Nadu. Worship here reaches back to the Tevaram age, but the stone buildings visible today are mostly of the Nayak period, raised over an earlier foundation whose builders are not firmly recorded.
sections.architecture: The temple is modest in scale, with a single gopuram, an entrance mandapa, and two circumambulatory corridors enclosing the shrines, its detail mostly Nayak and post-Vijayanagara in character. The sanctum of Kadambavaneswarar holds a self-manifested linga that faces north, an uncommon orientation, and behind it stand carved figures of seven celestial maidens, the Sapta Kannikas, shown in worship. The goddess Mutrila Mulaiammai has her own shrine within the enclosure. The sacred tree is the kadamba, from which the temple takes its name, and the sacred water is the Kaveri itself, flowing close beside the walls.
sections.legends: Two traditions explain the Lord's name. In the first, Shiva appeared in the kadamba forest before the sage Kanva, and the place came to be called Kadambanthurai. In the second, seven celestial maidens prayed to Shiva in this forest for protection from the demon Doomralochana, and the Lord destroyed the demon to save them and the grove, earning the title Lord of the Kadamba Forest. The maidens are still shown standing behind the linga, turned toward him in prayer. Both stories remember a forest sanctuary on the river, protected by the Lord for those who took refuge there.
sections.festivals: Thai Poosam is the great day of Kulithalai: the deities of the neighbouring Shiva temples are brought in procession to the Kaveri, and a vast crowd, said to be around two lakh, gathers on its banks. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed here as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Kulithalai is best approached as the first of a day's three offerings. Come in the morning, bathe your hands and feet in the Kaveri, and enter the quiet old enclosure to pray before the north-facing Lord, then turn to the goddess Mutrila Mulaiammai in her shrine. Pilgrims then traditionally go on to the hill temple of Ratnagiriswarar at Ayyarmalai in the afternoon and Thiruvengoimalai in the evening. Between the river, the kadamba tree and the old corridors, the temple has the unhurried feeling of a riverside sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to early afternoon and again from late afternoon into the evening; sources differ on exact hours, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Kulithalai lies on the Tiruchirappalli–Karur road and rail line on the bank of the Kaveri, about 34 km from Tiruchirappalli and 42 km from Karur. Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport. The town has a railway station and frequent buses, and the temple stands near the Kaveri in the town.
